sections.label: The opening
sections.line: The articles came from long briefs, not prompts
sections.para: Over four weeks I sent about 65,000 words in 148 messages, 55,000 of them in voice memos, and the agent published 96,000 words through 123 releases. No article came from a one-line prompt. The key input is thirty-three pieces of earlier published writing, and the corrections fix briefs, not hallucinations.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Long memos and a published record drive the output
sections.para: In twenty-seven days 65,323 words went in and twenty-two articles of 96,451 words came out, with 26 research agents and 123 releases. Corrections arrived a median of thirty-eight minutes after a release and were carried in five. Most corrections were direction, framing, voice, vocabulary or scope, and the record behind the memos is what makes the agent fast.

sections.label: The question, and why it needs numbers
sections.line: Measuring the session beats asserting how the work happens
sections.para: A friend called the volume of text baffling, and the usual answer, that I write briefs and review drafts, is one people nod at and disbelieve. So the transcript was joined to the git history to count words in and out per article. The limits are stated: the transcript starts on 9 September and attribution is approximate outside hand-checked articles.

sections.label: What went in, and what came out
sections.line: Thirty-seven voice memos carried 85 percent of input
sections.para: Of 148 messages, thirty-seven memos held 55,473 words; forty-six messages were corrections. The agent produced twenty-two articles, 105 figures and 75,993 words back to me. Eight articles show the range, from the fractal graphs piece argued over five releases to the memory article done in one, and the words-out ratio of one to five is the least interesting number.

sections.label: What the corrections were
sections.line: Corrections set direction; they rarely fix hallucinations
sections.para: The corrections fall into direction (the folder-tree analogy), framing (the SaaS title went round four times), voice, vocabulary (blast radius beside footprint, a banned ladder word) and scope. Only one was a fact the agent got wrong, and it came from my own document. A model that can go in every direction needs someone with a direction.

sections.label: What the memos were standing on
sections.line: The memos stand on fifteen years of published writing
sections.para: The code review company article cites thirty-three pieces of earlier writing: the 2010 O2 Platform, a 2016 book, 107 posts on diniscruz.ai, 3,025 team markdown files and twenty-six earlier articles. The agent is fast because that record exists and is public. Without it a memo would yield a plausible essay with nothing underneath.

sections.label: The form, the workflow and the tools
sections.line: The productivity comes from a pipeline I control
sections.para: Behind the articles is an open source pipeline: markdown conventions, figures rendered from web pages, graph JSON, a build and a validator that blocks dead links, em-dashes and leaks. Its tools were built on the day they were needed, including the transcript parser and a paragraph diff tool. A team without that habit gets speed only on the first draft.

sections.label: The evidence, as a vault
sections.line: An evidence vault holds every number and corrected two
sections.para: Every figure is a file in a vault built by a data scientist agent and a developer agent in an afternoon: 266 record rows, 124 releases, twenty-eight corrections, nine views. It showed corrections arrive within the hour and research agents ran only on publishing days. It also caught a double-counted compaction figure and an inflated message count.

sections.label: Why this is a better universe to learn from
sections.line: A published trail of ideas teaches models better
sections.para: Publishing the trail, wrong versions included, gives provenance and also a better learning source than a vector database of everything. Articles that cite each other, with graphs and correction records, give a model structure, which let the agent connect ideas I had not. The vault is therefore the next brief, and the vaults, graphs and diffs are the product.

sections.label: The compounding
sections.line: Each article compounds on the ones before it
sections.para: Seventeen of twenty-seven earlier articles cite another, with sixty-five links, and per-article graphs let the agent read selectively. Corrections compound into build rules, and eleven context compactions were recovered from the published record. Experts are not displaced: their direction, taste and experience are the input, and the same loop scales architects and reviewers.

sections.label: What is open
sections.line: The measurement has stated gaps and could improve
sections.para: The articles could be shorter, and attribution is hand-checked for only eight of them, with a heuristic for the rest. The 2010 to 2016 record is quoted but not counted, and the diniscruz.ai count is of posts, not words. The biggest input, the conversations and work behind the memos, is in no record.

sections.label: The article as one page, by another model
sections.line: A ChatGPT infographic has two numbers wrong
sections.para: Dinis asked ChatGPT for an infographic twice; the second leads with the idea that a model needs someone with a direction. The headline figures are right, but it gives 5,785 words of input for the code review company article and nineteen citing articles where the build says seventeen.
